q: 139. The maximum differential settlement is isolated footings on clayey soils should be limited to
explain: As per IS code guidance for isolated footings on clayey soils, the permissible differential settlement is typically limited to about 40 mm to avoid structural distress.

q: 140. A combined footing is generally used when
options: Number of columns is more than two and they are spaced far apart
Number of columns is two and they are spaced far close to each other
Number of columns is two and they are spaced far apart
explain: A combined footing is provided when two columns are close enough that their individual isolated footings would overlap, so a single combined footing supports both.

q: 141. Lime stabilization is very effective in treating
explain: Lime reacts with clay minerals (pozzolanic reaction) to reduce plasticity and swelling, making it most effective for plastic clayey soils.

q: 142. The bearing capacity of a strip footing on a saturated clay is 120 kN/m². The bearing capacity of a circular footing (diameter = width) will be
explain: For saturated clay (φ=0 condition), the shape factor increases bearing capacity for circular/square footings compared to a strip footing (Nc for circular > Nc for strip), so it will be more than 120 kN/m².

q: 143. A plate load test is useful to estimate
options: Both bearing capacity and settlement of foundation
explain: The plate load test provides a load-settlement curve from which both the safe bearing capacity and the expected settlement of the actual foundation can be estimated.

q: 144. A shallow foundation is defined as a foundation which
options: Has a depth of embedment less than its width
Is resting on the ground surface
explain: By Terzaghi's definition, a foundation is 'shallow' when its depth of embedment (Df) is less than or approximately equal to its width (B), typically Df ≤ B.

q: 145. The shear strength of very plastic cohesive soils can be found by
explain: The vane shear test is specifically suited for soft, very plastic, saturated cohesive soils where sampling for a triaxial/UCS test may be difficult.

q: 146. A fine grained soil has
explain: Fine-grained soils (clays/silts) have small pore sizes restricting flow (low permeability) and a compressible, plastic structure (high compressibility).

q: 147. The soil transported by water and deposited along the stream is called
explain: Alluvial soil is specifically the material carried and deposited by flowing river/stream water along its course.

q: 148. Three phase diagram of soil represents
options: Dust, fine sand and coarse sand
explain: The standard three-phase diagram used in soil mechanics divides soil mass into solids, water, and air — the three fundamental constituents.

q: 149. Graphical method for the determination of earth pressure
explain: Culmann's graphical method is a well-known trial-wedge construction technique for determining active/passive earth pressure, especially for irregular backfill conditions.

q: 150. According to IS code the soil having coefficient of permeability between 104 cm/sec. and 10-2 cm/sec. is termed as
explain: IS classification places soils with permeability in this intermediate range (between highly pervious and impervious) into the semi-pervious category.

q: 151. The angle that Coulomb's failure envelope makes with the horizontal is called
explain: In a Mohr-Coulomb shear strength plot, the slope of the failure envelope line with the horizontal (normal stress) axis is the angle of internal friction, φ.

q: 152. In a triaxial compression test on a soil specimen, the intermediate principal stress is equal to
options: Difference between major and minor principal stresses
explain: In the standard axisymmetric triaxial test, the confining (cell) pressure acts equally in both horizontal directions, so the intermediate principal stress equals the minor principal stress (σ2 = σ3).

q: 153. If the shearing stress is zero on two planes, then the angle between the two planes is
explain: Zero shear stress occurs only on the principal planes, and the two principal planes (major and minor) are always oriented at 90° to each other.

q: 154. Sensitivity of a soil can be defined as
options: Percentage of volume change of soil under saturated condition
Ratio of compressive strength of unconfined undisturbed soil to that of soil in a remolded state
Ratio of volume of voids to volume to solids
explain: Sensitivity St = (unconfined compressive strength, undisturbed) / (unconfined compressive strength, remoulded at same water content), indicating strength loss upon remoulding.

q: 155. Rankin's theory of earth pressure assumes that, back of the wall is
explain: Rankine's theory assumes the back face of the retaining wall is vertical and perfectly smooth (frictionless), simplifying the stress analysis to principal stress conditions.

q: 156. The coefficient of active earth pressure for loose sand having an angle of internal friction of 30° is
157. Coefficient of earth pressure at rest is
options: Less than active earth pressure but greater than passive earth pressure
Greater than active earth pressure but less than passive earth pressure
Greater than both the active earth pressure and passive earth pressure
Less than both the active and passive earth pressure
explain: Since Ka < K0 < Kp always (no wall movement gives an intermediate at-rest state between the minimum active and maximum passive states), K0 is greater than Ka but less than Kp.

q: 158. Cohesive soils are
options: Good for backfill because of low lateral pressure
Good for backfill because of high shear strength
Poor for backfill because of large lateral pressure
explain: Cohesive soils develop higher lateral earth pressures (and can absorb water causing swelling pressures), making them poor choices for retaining wall backfill compared to free-draining granular material.

q: 159. Which of the following earth pressure theories is directly applicable to bulk-heads?
explain: Neither Rankine's nor Coulomb's classical earth pressure theory directly accounts for the flexible, anchored/embedded behaviour of sheet-pile bulkheads, which require specialized bulkhead design methods.

q: 160. The densification of a soil by means of mechanical manipulation is
explain: Compaction is the process of densifying soil by mechanical means (rolling, tamping, vibration) to expel air, distinct from consolidation which involves expulsion of water over time.

q: 161. The curve showing the relationship between the dry unit weight and the water content of a soil for a given compactive effort, is called
explain: This is precisely the definition of the compaction (moisture-density) curve obtained from a Proctor test.

q: 162. A comparatively sudden reduction in volume of a soil mass under an applied load (due principally to expulsion and compression of gas in the soil voids preceding primary consolidation) is called
explain: This rapid initial volume reduction, occurring due to compression/expulsion of air before true primary consolidation begins, is termed initial consolidation.

q: 163. The angle between the abscissa and the tangent to the curve representing the relationship of shearing resistance to normal stress acting within a soil is called
explain: The slope of the shear stress vs normal stress curve (Mohr-Coulomb envelope) with the horizontal axis is, by definition, the angle of internal friction.

q: 164. The force of attraction between the individual particles of soil which keeps the soil particles bound together is known as
explain: Cohesion is defined as the inter-particle attractive force (electro-chemical bonding, especially in clays) that holds soil particles together independent of normal stress.

q: 165. The expansion of soil due to shear at a constant pressure is called as
explain: Dilatancy is the volumetric expansion that dense granular soils undergo when sheared, as particles ride over one another, even under constant confining pressure.

q: 166. Pile foundation are suitable for
explain: Piles are primarily used to transfer structural loads down through weak upper soil layers to a firm, competent bearing stratum below (end-bearing piles).

q: 167. Well foundations in sandy soils derive their bearing capacity from
explain: In cohesionless sandy strata, well foundations rely mainly on point (end) bearing resistance at the base rather than skin friction along the shaft.

q: 168. Core-cutter method is used for
options: Obtaining samples for direct shear test
explain: The core-cutter method is a standard field technique for determining the in-situ (dry/bulk) density of cohesive soils by driving a known-volume cutter into the ground.

q: 169. Agent responsible for the transportation of soil is
explain: Soil transportation and deposition can occur via wind (aeolian), water (alluvial/lacustrine/marine), or gravity (talus/colluvial) — all are recognized transporting agents.

q: 170. In hydrometer analysis, equation is derived based on
explain: Hydrometer analysis (for fine-grained particle-size distribution) uses Stoke's law, which relates the terminal settling velocity of spherical particles in a fluid to their diameter.

q: 171. Consolidation is a process involving
explain: Consolidation is a slow, time-dependent process in which excess pore water pressure dissipates and water is gradually squeezed out of a saturated soil under sustained load.

q: 172. Standard Proctor test is used for determining
explain: The Standard Proctor compaction test establishes the relationship between dry density and moisture content, identifying the optimum moisture content for maximum compaction.

q: 173. Compaction or Soil is aimed at
explain: Compaction packs soil particles more closely together, reducing the void ratio (and expelling air), which in turn increases dry density and shear strength.

q: 174. The most effective method for compacting sands is by
explain: Cohesionless sandy soils compact best under vibratory action (vibrating rollers/plates), which rearranges the granular particles into a denser packing.

q: 175. Plasticity needle is used to determine
options: Plastic limit of the soil used in compaction
Penetration resistance to control field compaction
Penetration value of bitumen used in road construction
Swelling index of black cotton soils
explain: The plasticity/proctor needle is a field device used to measure penetration resistance, helping control and verify field compaction quality against the laboratory compaction curve.

q: 176. Bitumen, when added to soil, mainly
explain: Bitumen stabilization primarily works by coating soil particles to reduce water absorption and infiltration, essentially acting as a waterproofing/binding agent.

q: 177. An isobar is
options: Point below ground surface where net pressure is zero
A curve or contour connecting all points below ground surface of equal vertical stress
A curve or contour connecting all points below ground surface of equal horizontal stress
A location where vertical stress is equal to horizontal stress
explain: An isobar (pressure bulb contour) in soil mechanics connects points of equal vertical stress increase caused by a surface load, used to visualize the pressure bulb beneath a footing.

q: 178. For calculating stress distribution in soils, Boussinesq assumed point load to be
explain: Boussinesq's classical elastic theory for stress distribution assumes a concentrated point load applied at the ground surface (ground level) of a semi-infinite, homogeneous, isotropic elastic medium.

q: 179. Van Shear test is used for
options: Measuring shear strength of Cohesive soil of low shear strength
Measuring void ratio of sandy soils
explain: The vane shear test is specifically designed to measure the undrained shear strength of soft, saturated cohesive soils with low shear strength, in-situ or in the lab.

q: 180. Thixotropy refers to
options: Flow of highly viscous fluids through soil
Increase in thickness of soil fabric
explain: Thixotropy is the phenomenon where a remoulded clay soil, left undisturbed at constant water content, gradually regains (increases) part of its lost strength over time.

q: 181. Hydraulic gradient provided at the downstream side of a hydraulic structures such as dam is called
explain: The hydraulic gradient at the point where seepage water exits the ground on the downstream side of a dam/structure is called the exit gradient, critical for piping/uplift checks.

q: 182. Units of co-efficient of permeability
explain: Coefficient of permeability k has units of velocity (length/time), commonly expressed as cm/sec, since it represents flow velocity under unit hydraulic gradient.

q: 183. Falling head permeability test is preferable when soil sample is
explain: The falling head test suits fine-grained soils (clays) with low permeability, where the small, slow water flow can be accurately measured by the falling head in a standpipe, unlike the constant head test used for sandy soils.

q: 184. Quick sand is
options: A condition in which cohesion is decreased quickly
A sand which can be compacted quickly
A condition in which a cohesionless soil loses its strength because of upward flow of water
explain: Quicksand is not a soil type but a hydraulic condition: upward seepage pressure equals or exceeds the submerged unit weight of a cohesionless soil, reducing effective stress and shear strength to near zero.

q: 185. Maximum failures of earth dams are due to
options: Erosion of soil due to flowing water
Leakage through cavities or holes formed by animals
explain: Historically, the most common cause of earth dam failure is erosion/piping of soil caused by uncontrolled seepage/overtopping flowing water eroding the embankment.

q: 186. In a flow net
options: Flow lines and equipotential lines meet at right angles to one another
Quantity of water flowing through each flow channel is different
Larger the dimensions of the field, smaller will be the hydraulic gradient
Different potential drop occurs between two successive equipotential lines
explain: A defining property of a properly constructed flow net is that flow lines and equipotential lines always intersect orthogonally (at right angles), forming curvilinear squares.

q: 187. Consolidation theory was due to
explain: Karl Terzaghi formulated the classical one-dimensional theory of consolidation, a cornerstone of modern soil mechanics.

q: 188. Sheet piles are held in position by
options: Adjusting water level on one side
explain: Anchored sheet pile walls are stabilized primarily through tie rods connected to anchors set back in stable ground, in addition to embedment, but tie rods are the key holding mechanism cited here.

q: 189. Caissons are structures used for
options: Dewatering while laying foundations in proper position
explain: Caissons are large prefabricated box/well structures sunk into the ground/water to allow foundations to be constructed properly in position, especially below water or through soft strata.

q: 190. Stability number is given by
explain: Per Taylor's stability chart formulation, the dimensionless stability number is expressed as Sn = C²/H in this book's given equation form.

q: 191. Consolidation is a process involving
explain: Consolidation is defined by the slow, time-dependent, gradual expulsion of pore water from saturated soil under sustained load, not sudden or abnormal effects.

q: 192. Density index for a natural soil is used to express
explain: Density index (relative density) expresses how compact/dense a granular soil is in its natural state compared to its loosest and densest possible states.

q: 193. Factor of safety of embankments shall be
explain: For slope stability of embankments against shear failure, a factor of safety of at least 2.5 (or similar high value per this reference) is typically recommended for safety.

q: 194. Shallow footing is one whose depth is
explain: Per Terzaghi's definition, a shallow foundation has depth less than or equal to (approximately) its width, not strictly less than, more than, or always equal — hence 'none of the above' as per the book's answer.

q: 195. Value of factor of safety adopted in foundation design is
explain: For bearing capacity calculations in foundation design, a factor of safety in the range of 2.5 to 3.0 is conventionally adopted to account for uncertainties.

q: 196. The maximum size of plate for plate load test is
explain: As per standard plate load test procedure, the test plate size typically ranges up to about 60 cm (square/circular), used to simulate the foundation's bearing behaviour.

q: 197. A fully saturated soil is said to be
options: Two phase system with soil and air
Two phase system with soil and water
explain: When all void spaces are filled entirely with water (no air), the soil reduces to a two-phase system of solids and water only.

q: 198. A soil has a bulk density of 22kN/m3 and water content 10%. The dry density of soil is
199. If the volume of voids is equal to the volume of solids in a soil mass, then the values of porosity and voids ratio respectively are
explain: If Vv = Vs, then void ratio e = Vv/Vs = 1.0, and porosity n = Vv/(Vv+Vs) = 1/2 = 0.5, giving porosity=0.5 and void ratio=1.0.

q: 200. If the, degree of saturation of a partially saturated soil is 60%, then air content of the soil is
explain: Air content = 1 - degree of saturation (as fraction of voids) = 100% - 60% = 40%, since air and water together fill 100% of the void space.

q: 201. When the plasticity index of a soil is zero, the soil is
explain: A zero plasticity index means the soil shows no plastic range (liquid limit ≈ plastic limit or cannot be determined), characteristic of non-plastic cohesionless soils like sand.

q: 202. Relative density of a compacted dense sand is approximately equal to
explain: A well-compacted, dense sand approaches its densest possible state (e close to emin), giving a relative density close to but just under 1.0, i.e., approximately 0.95.

q: 203. Which of the following methods is most accurate for the determination of the water content of soil'
explain: The oven drying method (at 105-110°C to constant weight) remains the standard reference/most accurate laboratory method for water content determination.

q: 204. A pycnometer is used to determine
explain: A pycnometer determines the specific gravity of soil solids directly, and (for soils of known G) can also be used to back-calculate water content.

q: 205. Stoke's law is valid only if the size of particle is
explain: Stoke's law (for laminar settling used in hydrometer analysis) is valid within the particle size range of roughly 0.2 mm down to 0.0002 mm; outside this range turbulence or Brownian motion invalidates it.

q: 206. Shearing strength of a cohesionless soil depends upon
explain: For a purely frictional cohesionless soil, shear strength (s = σ tanφ) is fundamentally governed by the normal stress on the failure plane.

q: 207. Honey combed structure is found in
explain: An open honeycomb arrangement of particles, bridged by inter-particle bonding, typically develops in fine silts and clays during sedimentation.
